Missing source control (undrained collection) - antibiotics alone will fail

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship
UKHSA Start Smart Then Focus antimicrobial stewardship toolkit

title: Avoiding redundant anaerobic cover
summary: Double anaerobic cover (e.g. adding metronidazole to an agent that already has good anaerobic activity) is a common, avoidable prescribing error. It adds toxicity and cost, broadens the spectrum unnecessarily, and increases C. difficile risk without benefit.

sections.heading: Agents with inherent anaerobic activity
items: Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate)
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Carbapenems (e.g. meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem)
Metronidazole and clindamycin (dedicated anaerobic agents)
Moxifloxacin (among fluoroquinolones, has anaerobic activity)

steps.detail: Do NOT add metronidazole to co-amoxiclav, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem for anaerobic cover - the base agent already covers anaerobes.
Identify and stop redundant anaerobic agents on the antimicrobial review; document the rationale.

redFlags: Metronidazole co-prescribed with co-amoxiclav, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem (redundant) - stop the metronidazole unless a specific indication exists (e.g. confirmed C. difficile or a specific protocol)

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship
WHO AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) classification of antibiotics

title: Double (empirical) Gram-negative cover: when and when not
summary: Empirical combination therapy with two Gram-negative-active agents (e.g. a beta-lactam plus an aminoglycoside) is sometimes used in severe sepsis to broaden the chance of covering a resistant organism. Routine prolonged double cover, however, adds toxicity and resistance pressure without consistent mortality benefit and should be de-escalated.

sections.heading: Principles
items: The main rationale for empirical double Gram-negative cover is to increase the likelihood of adequate initial coverage in severe sepsis where resistant Gram-negatives are plausible (e.g. neutropenic sepsis, known multidrug-resistant colonisation, local resistance)
It is NOT reliably shown to improve outcomes through 'synergy' for most infections and increases nephrotoxicity (aminoglycosides) and resistance selection
Once susceptibilities are known, de-escalate to a single effective agent

steps.detail: Reserve empirical double cover for defined high-risk scenarios per local guidelines; do not use routinely.
At 48-72h, stop the second agent (e.g. the aminoglycoside) once the organism is identified and susceptible to a single agent.

redFlags: Prolonged empirical double Gram-negative cover without de-escalation - toxicity and resistance with no added benefit
Continuing an aminoglycoside beyond a few days without TDM and renal monitoring
Using combination therapy as a substitute for getting cultures and reviewing

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship

title: Vancomycin therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)
summary: Vancomycin requires therapeutic drug monitoring to balance efficacy against nephrotoxicity. Current guidance favours AUC-guided dosing (target AUC/MIC 400-600 mg.h/L), commonly using Bayesian software or two-level (peak and trough) estimation, with a loading dose in serious infection.

sections.heading: Targets and method
items: Preferred target: AUC/MIC 400-600 mg.h/L (assuming MIC 1 mg/L), estimated by Bayesian software (gold standard) or two-concentration kinetics
Trough-only monitoring is the older approach; AUC-guided dosing reduces nephrotoxicity for similar efficacy
TDM is indicated for essentially all patients expected to receive vancomycin beyond ~48 hours, and earlier in unstable renal function or serious infection

steps.detail: Give a weight-based loading dose in serious infection to reach therapeutic levels quickly, then maintenance dosing by renal function.
Check levels at the appropriate time, monitor renal function regularly, and adjust dose to keep within target while avoiding accumulation.

redFlags: Rising creatinine / acute kidney injury on vancomycin (especially with other nephrotoxins e.g. aminoglycosides, piperacillin-tazobactam) - review dose and target
Subtherapeutic levels in serious infection (e.g. MRSA bacteraemia, endocarditis) - risk of failure
Dosing without TDM beyond 48 hours

references.label: Introductory Guide to Therapeutic Drug Monitoring for Vancomycin AUC (PrecisePK summary of ASHP/IDSA guidance)

title: Aminoglycoside (gentamicin) dosing and TDM
summary: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent bactericidal agents usually given as once-daily (extended-interval) dosing (e.g. gentamicin ~5-7 mg/kg) to maximise the high peak that drives killing while allowing a drug-free trough that limits nephro- and ototoxicity. Levels must be monitored and renal function tracked.

sections.heading: Dosing and monitoring
items: Once-daily (extended-interval) dosing, e.g. gentamicin ~5-7 mg/kg, has largely replaced multiple daily dosing for most indications

Monitor with a single timed level plotted on a nomogram (e.g. Hartford / Barnes-Jewish), or measure trough; aim for a low/undetectable trough (commonly <1 mg/L) before the next dose to allow renal recovery

Use ideal/adjusted body weight for dosing and dose by renal function; extended-interval dosing is generally avoided in pregnancy, significant renal impairment, endocarditis (synergy regimens), and major burns - use divided-dose monitoring there

steps.detail: Keep courses short; aminoglycoside toxicity is cumulative - review the need daily and stop/de-escalate at 48-72h.
Check renal function regularly and ask about ototoxicity/vestibular symptoms; hold or adjust if the trough is high or renal function worsens.

redFlags: High pre-dose (trough) level or rising creatinine - withhold/extend interval (risk of nephrotoxicity)
New hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo - possible ototoxicity, reassess
Prolonged aminoglycoside therapy without TDM and renal monitoring

references.label: Gentamicin: dose regimens and monitoring (The Pharmaceutical Journal)

title: Antifungal stewardship basics
summary: Antifungal stewardship promotes appropriate diagnosis, choice, route, duration and de-escalation of antifungals. Invasive candidiasis is commonly oversuspected yet underdiagnosed, leading to overuse; structured review and de-escalation (e.g. echinocandin to fluconazole) reduce consumption, toxicity, interactions and cost.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Confirm/refute fungal infection with appropriate sampling and tests (cultures, susceptibilities, biomarkers such as beta-D-glucan/mannan where available)
Echinocandins are often preferred empirically in unstable/critically ill patients with suspected invasive candidiasis

De-escalation: switch from an echinocandin to fluconazole (when the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible, the patient is stable and source-controlled, and blood cultures clear) - typically within a few days
Stop empirical antifungals if invasive infection is not supported by tests and the patient is improving

steps.detail: Reassess the indication, results and response; de-escalate, switch IV to oral, or stop as appropriate.
Involve microbiology/infection specialists for invasive fungal disease, resistant isolates, and choice/duration of therapy.

redFlags: Empirical antifungal continued without confirmed infection in an improving patient with negative tests - stop
Echinocandin continued when step-down to fluconazole is appropriate (susceptible isolate, stable, source controlled)
Resistant or unusual fungal isolate - specialist advice

references.label: Antifungal stewardship with an emphasis on candidaemia (ScienceDirect)
Antifungal stewardship in critically ill patients (Intensive Care Med, PMC)

title: Restricted-antibiotic approval and ward audit basics
summary: Antimicrobial stewardship programmes restrict access to broad-spectrum/last-line agents (WHO Watch and especially Reserve groups) via approval or pre-authorisation, and use prospective audit and feedback to improve prescribing. These are core, evidence-based stewardship interventions.

sections.heading: Restriction / pre-authorisation
items: Require specialist (microbiology/infection) approval before, or shortly after, starting restricted agents (typically Watch and Reserve antibiotics, e.g. carbapenems, colistin, linezolid)
Approval ensures the indication is appropriate and an alternative narrower agent is not suitable, and sets a review/stop date
Aligns with WHO AWaRe: maximise Access-group use; restrict and monitor Watch/Reserve

steps.detail: Stewardship/pharmacy teams review active antimicrobial prescriptions on the ward against documented indication, guideline concordance, allergy status, dose/route, and review date.
Give prescribers timely feedback with recommendations (stop, de-escalate, IV-to-oral switch, set duration); track metrics (e.g. % Access-group use, point-prevalence) to drive improvement.

redFlags: Reserve-group antibiotic used without specialist approval/review
Restricted antibiotic continued past its review date without documented justification
Poor documentation of indication, allergy, or stop/review date on audit

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship: systems and processes
WHO AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) classification of antibiotics

title: Pain assessment tools
summary: Pain is what the patient says it is; structured tools improve consistency of assessment and response monitoring. Choose the tool to match the patient's communication and cognitive ability - self-report scales for those who can communicate, and validated observational/behavioural scales for those who cannot.

sections.heading: Self-report scales (preferred when able)
items: Numeric Rating Scale (NRS): patient rates pain 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst imaginable)
Visual Analogue Scale (VAS): mark on a 10 cm line
Verbal Rating Scale (VRS): none / mild / moderate / severe
Wong-Baker FACES scale: faces from happy to crying - useful for children and some adults

sections.heading: Observational tools for non-verbal patients
items: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability): observational scale for young children and non-verbal patients
PAINAD (Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia): five behavioural indicators scored 0-10 over a short observation period
Abbey Pain Scale: behavioural pain assessment in people with advanced dementia

steps.detail: Use a structured approach (e.g. site, onset, character, radiation, associations, timing, exacerbating/relieving factors, severity) and assess for neuropathic features and total/holistic pain.
Use the same tool to track response to analgesia and titrate; document scores over time.

redFlags: New severe or rapidly escalating pain - reassess for a treatable cause (e.g. fracture, cord compression, obstruction)
Unrecognised pain in non-verbal patients - use a validated observational tool, do not assume absence of pain

references.label: Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia Scale (PAINAD)
Pain assessment tools in paediatric palliative care: systematic review (PMC)

title: Opioid side-effect management
summary: Most opioid side effects (nausea, drowsiness) are common at initiation and on dose increase but improve with tolerance over days - except constipation, which persists and must be managed throughout. Anticipating and treating side effects improves adherence and comfort.

sections.heading: Common side effects and management
items: Constipation: does NOT improve with tolerance - co-prescribe a regular laxative (e.g. stimulant +/- softener/osmotic) from the start
Nausea/vomiting: common on starting/increasing - often transient; offer a regular antiemetic (e.g. haloperidol or metoclopramide) for the first days, then review
Drowsiness/sedation: common initially and after dose increases, usually settles in a few days; warn about driving
Dry mouth: frequent - mouth care, sips/sprays
Pruritus, sweating, myoclonus (at higher doses) - consider opioid switch if troublesome

steps.detail: Persistent/increasing drowsiness, confusion, vivid dreams/hallucinations, myoclonic jerks, pinpoint pupils and reduced respiratory rate suggest opioid toxicity (consider accumulation, e.g. in renal impairment).
Reduce/hold the dose, ensure hydration, treat reversible causes; in severe respiratory depression give titrated naloxone. Consider opioid rotation for persistent intolerable effects.

redFlags: Reduced respiratory rate, pinpoint pupils, increasing drowsiness/confusion or myoclonus - opioid toxicity; hold opioid, treat, titrated naloxone if severe
Worsening function in renal impairment (morphine metabolite accumulation) - consider dose reduction or an alternative opioid
Uncontrolled constipation / impaction

references.label: NICE CG140 Palliative care for adults: strong opioids for pain relief

title: Methadone in palliative care: cautions
summary: Methadone can be valuable for complex/neuropathic cancer pain but is high-risk: it has a long and highly variable half-life, a variable (non-linear) conversion ratio from other opioids, and a risk of QT prolongation. Initiation and opioid rotation to methadone should be specialist-led.

sections.heading: Why methadone needs caution
items: Long and variable half-life (roughly 15-150 hours): dose changes can take more than 3 days to reach full effect, with a risk of accumulation, sedation and respiratory depression
Conversion from other opioids is variable and dose-dependent (NOT a fixed ratio) - standard equianalgesic tables do not apply reliably
Risk of QT-interval prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially at higher doses, IV use, with other QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte disturbance
Many drug interactions via hepatic metabolism

steps.detail: Restrict initiation and opioid rotation to methadone to clinicians with palliative/pain expertise; do not switch using simple equianalgesic conversion.
Consider baseline and follow-up ECG (QTc) where appropriate, correct electrolytes, review interacting/QT-prolonging drugs, and titrate slowly with close monitoring for accumulation.

redFlags: Increasing sedation/respiratory depression days after a dose change (accumulation due to long half-life)
QTc prolongation, syncope, or co-prescribed QT-prolonging drugs/electrolyte disturbance
Non-specialist conversion to methadone using standard equianalgesic ratios

Practical Guide for Using Methadone in Pain and Palliative Care Practice (PMC)

title: Syringe driver (subcutaneous infusion) drug compatibility
summary: A continuous subcutaneous infusion via syringe driver delivers symptom-control drugs when the oral route fails. Mixing drugs risks physical/chemical incompatibility (e.g. precipitation), and the risk rises with the number of drugs and their concentrations - always check a compatibility resource before combining.

sections.heading: Diluent and compatibility principles
items: Common diluents are water for injection or sodium chloride 0.9%; choice depends on the drugs (0.9% saline is closer to physiological tonicity and may reduce site irritation)
Cyclizine should be diluted with WATER for injection - it precipitates with saline and at higher concentrations (e.g. above ~10 mg/mL or with higher diamorphine concentrations)
Incompatibility risk increases with more drugs and higher concentrations in the syringe
Inspect the syringe regularly for cloudiness, precipitation, or discolouration and discard if seen

steps.detail: Always consult a recognised syringe-driver compatibility chart/resource for the specific drug combination, diluent and concentrations before preparing the infusion.
If drugs are incompatible (e.g. cyclizine with high-dose diamorphine), use a separate syringe driver or an alternative agent (e.g. levomepromazine as a single daily SC injection).

redFlags: Cloudiness/precipitation or discolouration in the syringe - discard and re-prepare; do not infuse
Combining cyclizine with saline or high diamorphine concentrations (precipitation)
Site reaction/poor absorption - rotate the site and review the diluent

references.label: Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines: syringe pump compatibility and stability tables
Syringe Drivers: Subcutaneous (SC) Drug Infusion (Patient.info professional)

title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
summary: Hypercalcaemia is a common metabolic emergency in advanced cancer, causing nausea, constipation, polyuria, thirst, confusion and drowsiness. Mainstay treatment is vigorous IV rehydration with 0.9% saline followed by an IV bisphosphonate; always interpret the corrected (albumin-adjusted) calcium.

sections.heading: Recognition
items: Symptoms ('stones, bones, groans, moans'): nausea/vomiting, constipation, polyuria and thirst, fatigue, confusion, drowsiness; can progress to coma
Use the corrected (albumin-adjusted) calcium; treat symptomatic hypercalcaemia or markedly raised levels
Common in myeloma and breast, lung and squamous cancers (often via PTHrP)

steps.detail: IV 0.9% sodium chloride to restore intravascular volume and promote calciuresis (e.g. several litres/24h, adjusted for cardiac/renal status) - the first and most urgent step.
After rehydration give an IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid, dose-adjusted for renal function); calcium falls over ~2-4 days with maximal effect by ~5-7 days, lasting weeks.
Bisphosphonates may be inappropriate if prognosis is very short (effect is delayed). Consider denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory or contraindicated; treat the underlying cancer where feasible.

redFlags: Drowsiness, confusion, or coma with hypercalcaemia - emergency, urgent rehydration
Markedly raised corrected calcium (e.g. >=3.0 mmol/L) - treat promptly
Renal impairment - adjust bisphosphonate dose and rehydrate carefully

references.label: Hypercalcemia of Malignancy (Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin Fast Fact)
Treatment of hypercalcaemia of malignancy in adults (PMC)

title: Malignant bowel obstruction (palliative)
summary: Malignant bowel obstruction in advanced cancer is often managed medically when surgery or stenting is not appropriate. The aim is to control pain, nausea/vomiting and colic. Antisecretory, antiemetic, anti-inflammatory and analgesic drugs are combined and given by the subcutaneous route.

sections.heading: Medical (conservative) management
items: Assess for surgery, stenting or venting where appropriate; medical management is for inoperable/unfit patients
Pain: opioid analgesia (continuous SC infusion); for colic, an antispasmodic/antisecretory antimuscarinic (e.g. hyoscine butylbromide) and AVOID prokinetics in complete obstruction

Nausea/vomiting: antiemetic - haloperidol or, for complete obstruction, an antisecretory approach; metoclopramide may help in incomplete obstruction without colic but should be stopped if colic worsens
Reduce secretions: hyoscine butylbromide or octreotide (somatostatin analogue) to reduce GI secretions and vomiting
Dexamethasone may help relieve obstruction (reduces bowel-wall oedema) and acts as an antiemetic

steps.detail: Deliver drugs by continuous subcutaneous infusion (oral route unreliable); a common combination is an antiemetic + antisecretory agent +/- dexamethasone + opioid.
Treat dry mouth and thirst with mouth care/sips; consider venting gastrostomy or NG tube for refractory vomiting; reassess regularly.

redFlags: Use of a prokinetic (e.g. metoclopramide) or stimulant laxative in COMPLETE obstruction - can worsen colic/perforation risk, avoid
Signs of strangulation/perforation (severe constant pain, peritonism, sepsis) - urgent surgical review
Refractory vomiting - consider octreotide and venting decompression

references.label: MASCC multidisciplinary recommendations for management of malignant bowel obstruction (Support Care Cancer 2022)

title: Malignant spinal cord compression (palliative emergency)
summary: Malignant spinal cord (or cauda equina) compression is an oncological emergency. Outcome depends on speed of treatment, so suspect it early in any cancer patient with new or worsening back pain or neurological signs. Give high-dose dexamethasone immediately and arrange urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours.

sections.heading: Recognition (red flags)
items: New or progressive back pain (often the earliest symptom), especially band-like, worse on lying/straining, or thoracic
Radicular pain, limb weakness, sensory level or sensory loss, gait disturbance
Bladder/bowel dysfunction (urinary retention/incontinence, faecal incontinence) - late and ominous
Known malignancy (commonly prostate, breast, lung, myeloma) raises suspicion

steps.detail: Give high-dose corticosteroid as soon as MSCC is suspected (e.g. dexamethasone 16 mg/day, often 8 mg twice daily) with gastroprotection (PPI) and monitor glucose - do not wait for imaging.
Arrange MRI of the WHOLE spine within 24 hours (multiple levels may be involved) to confirm and guide treatment.

Refer urgently for radiotherapy and/or surgical decompression per the MSCC pathway; flat bed rest / spinal precautions until instability is excluded, analgesia, thromboprophylaxis, and catheter if retention.

redFlags: New/worsening back pain or any neurological deficit in a cancer patient - treat as MSCC until excluded
Bladder or bowel dysfunction - late sign, act immediately
Delay in steroids or MRI - risks irreversible paralysis

title: Bereavement support
summary: Grief is a normal, individual response to loss; most bereaved people adapt with the support of family and community and do not need specialist intervention. Care involves acknowledging the loss, providing information and practical support, and identifying the minority who need additional or specialist help.

sections.heading: Principles and tiered support
items: Most bereaved people cope with support from family, friends and community (no formal intervention needed) - normalise and validate grief
Offer information, signposting to bereavement services, and practical guidance (e.g. what to do after a death)
Some need additional support (e.g. peer/volunteer or counselling); a minority with complex/prolonged grief or mental-health problems need specialist input
Tailor support to culture, faith and the individual; pay particular attention to children and to anticipated 'high-risk' grief (sudden death, dependent relationship, poor support)

steps.detail: Express condolence, listen, and assess coping, support and risk; recognise warning signs of complicated/prolonged grief or depression.
Provide written information and contacts for bereavement services; arrange follow-up and refer to specialist bereavement or mental-health services when indicated.

redFlags: Prolonged, intense, or disabling grief (e.g. persisting beyond expected, impairing function) - refer for specialist bereavement support
Suicidal ideation, severe depression, or psychosis - urgent mental-health assessment
Bereaved children or dependants needing dedicated support

references.label: WHO Palliative care (family and bereavement support)

title: Paediatric palliative care: principles
summary: Paediatric palliative care is active, holistic care of the child's body, mind and spirit and support for the family, beginning at diagnosis and continuing regardless of whether the child receives disease-directed treatment. It differs from adult care in its developmental, family-centred and long-trajectory nature.

sections.heading: Core principles (WHO)
items: Active total care of the child and support of the family, addressing physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs
Begins when illness is diagnosed and continues alongside curative/disease-directed treatment - not only end of life
Provided across settings (home, hospital, hospice) with a multidisciplinary team
Family-centred: parents and siblings are part of the unit of care, including bereavement support

steps.detail: Assessment and communication must be developmentally appropriate; use age-appropriate pain tools (e.g. FLACC, Wong-Baker FACES) and involve the child in decisions as appropriate.

Conditions span far beyond cancer (e.g. severe neurodisability, metabolic, congenital and organ-failure conditions) and trajectories may last years; weight-based dosing and specialist input are essential.
Provide practical, psychological and respite support, advance/parallel planning, and continuity, including support for siblings and after death.

redFlags: Uncontrolled symptoms (pain, seizures, breathlessness, distress) - escalate to specialist paediatric palliative care
Family distress, carer breakdown, or unmet sibling needs
Transitions of care (settings, or to adult services) without continuity planning

references.label: WHO Palliative care (definition for children)

title: Discharge medication counselling
summary: Clear counselling at discharge and accurate medicines reconciliation reduce errors, readmissions and harm. The patient (or carer) should leave understanding what each medicine is for, how and when to take it, what has changed, and what to watch for.

sections.heading: What to cover
items: Reconcile the list: compare pre-admission and discharge medicines; clearly flag what is new, changed, stopped, or time-limited (and why)
For each medicine: name, purpose, dose, route, timing, and how long to take it
Key side effects and what to do, plus important interactions and foods/alcohol to avoid
How to obtain ongoing supplies and any monitoring required (e.g. bloods, INR)
Use teach-back: ask the patient to explain the plan back to confirm understanding

steps.detail: Use plain language, consider health literacy/language needs, provide written information and a clear medication list, and address adherence aids (e.g. dosette) where helpful.
Communicate changes to the GP/community pharmacist, give clear safety-netting (when and who to contact), and arrange follow-up/monitoring.

redFlags: High-risk medicines (e.g. anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, methotrexate, lithium) without clear instructions and monitoring
Duplicate or omitted medicines after reconciliation
Patient unable to teach-back the plan, or no continuity/follow-up arranged

references.label: NICE NG5: Medicines optimisation (medicines reconciliation and self-management)

title: Warfarin: INR and diet counselling
summary: Warfarin's effect is monitored by the INR and is sensitive to vitamin K intake, alcohol, illness and many drugs. The dietary message is CONSISTENCY, not avoidance: keep vitamin K intake (mainly from green leafy vegetables) steady rather than cutting it out.

sections.heading: Diet and lifestyle
items: Do NOT avoid green leafy vegetables - keep your usual amount steady from week to week (sudden large changes in vitamin K alter the INR)
Major vitamin K sources: kale, spinach, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, lettuce
Avoid binge drinking and large swings in alcohol; cranberry/grapefruit juice can increase bleeding risk - be cautious
Tell any prescriber/pharmacist you take warfarin before starting/stopping medicines or herbal products (many interact); avoid OTC NSAIDs/aspirin unless advised

steps.detail: Take warfarin at the same time each day (commonly evening); attend regular INR checks and follow the recorded dose; more frequent INR checks are needed during illness, antibiotics, or diet changes.

steps.step: Know your INR and recognise bleeding
steps.detail: Carry an anticoagulant alert card/booklet; report signs of bleeding (see red flags). If a dose is missed, follow advice - do not double up without guidance.

redFlags: Signs of bleeding: blood in urine/stool (or black stools), coughing/vomiting blood, prolonged nosebleeds/gum bleeding, heavy or unusual bruising, severe headache - seek urgent medical advice
High INR or recent change in medicines/diet/illness - check INR and review dose
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic) - urgent review

references.label: Warfarin, your diet, and vitamin K foods (University of Iowa Health Care)

title: Steroid sick-day rules (adrenal insufficiency)
summary: People with adrenal insufficiency (primary, secondary, or on long-term steroids that suppress the axis) cannot mount a cortisol stress response and must increase their steroid dose during illness, injury or surgery to prevent a life-threatening adrenal crisis. They should carry a steroid emergency card and an emergency hydrocortisone injection.

sections.heading: Sick-day rules (oral, minor illness)
items: Fever/infection (temperature >=38C), or significant illness: take DOUBLE (or 2-3x) the usual oral glucocorticoid (e.g. hydrocortisone) for the duration of the illness, then return to normal
Diarrhoea without vomiting: double the dose until it settles
Vomiting: if a dose is vomited within ~30 minutes, repeat it; if vomiting continues / oral dose cannot be kept down, give the emergency IM injection and seek urgent care
Minor procedures/major stress: extra/parenteral steroid cover is needed - plan with the team

steps.detail: Severe weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness/confusion, hypotension/collapse - this is an emergency.
Give 100 mg hydrocortisone by IM (or IV) injection immediately, call emergency services stating 'adrenal crisis', and arrange hospital admission for IV hydrocortisone and IV 0.9% saline.
Patient/carers should be trained to give the emergency injection and carry a steroid emergency card and the injection kit at all times.

redFlags: Persistent vomiting/diarrhoea preventing oral steroid absorption - give IM hydrocortisone and seek urgent care
Signs of adrenal crisis (collapse, drowsiness, severe vomiting, hypotension) - 100 mg IM/IV hydrocortisone and emergency admission
Stopping long-term steroids abruptly - risk of adrenal crisis

references.label: Society for Endocrinology: adrenal insufficiency / steroid sick-day rules (patient information)

title: Personalised asthma action plan counselling
summary: A written personalised asthma action plan, developed with the patient, improves outcomes and reduces attacks and admissions. It commonly uses a traffic-light (green/amber/red) structure based on symptoms and/or peak flow against the person's personal best.

sections.heading: Traffic-light zones
items: GREEN (well controlled): no/minimal symptoms, peak flow ~80-100% of personal best - continue regular preventer (and reliever as prescribed)
AMBER (worsening): more symptoms, waking at night, needing reliever more, peak flow ~50-80% of best - follow the step-up instructions (e.g. increase treatment as advised) and seek review
RED (emergency): severe breathlessness, reliever not helping/needed very often, peak flow <50% of best, difficulty speaking - use reliever and get emergency help (call emergency services)

steps.detail: Record the person's regular medicines (preventer/reliever), personal-best peak flow, triggers, and exactly what to do in each zone, in their own plan.
Check and correct inhaler technique, confirm understanding of when to step up and seek help, and review the plan at every asthma contact and after any attack.

redFlags: Reliever needed very frequently or not lasting, peak flow <50% of best, too breathless to speak/eat, blue lips - emergency, call for help
Frequent reliever use / running out of reliever inhalers - poor control, urgent review
Any asthma attack - review and update the action plan and inhaler technique

references.label: American Lung Association: Create an Asthma Action Plan
Personalised asthma action plans for adults with asthma (PMC)

title: Epilepsy safety counselling
summary: Counselling people with epilepsy on everyday safety reduces seizure-related injury and the risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). Key areas are medication adherence, water safety, driving, heights/heat, and recognising and reducing personal risks.

sections.heading: Everyday safety advice
items: Water: shower rather than bath where possible (reduces drowning risk), use lukewarm water, do not lock the bathroom door, and avoid swimming alone (use the buddy system / supervision)
Driving: must meet the legal/licensing seizure-free requirements and inform the driving authority; do not drive if seizures are uncontrolled or medication causes impairing side effects
Heights, machinery and heat: take care with ladders/heights, dangerous machinery, and cooking (use back hob rings, guard against burns)
At home/work: consider seizure alarms for nocturnal seizures and tell people nearby what to do (seizure first aid)

steps.detail: Take antiseizure medication consistently and do NOT stop abruptly (a major risk factor for seizures and SUDEP); manage sleep deprivation, alcohol and other personal triggers.
Aim for the best achievable seizure control, review regularly, discuss SUDEP, and give individualised safety and first-aid advice to the person and family.

redFlags: Abrupt cessation of antiseizure medication - risk of seizures, status epilepticus and SUDEP
Convulsive seizure lasting >5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery (status epilepticus) - emergency
Driving against medical/legal advice; swimming or bathing unsupervised with uncontrolled seizures

references.label: Epilepsy Foundation: Staying Safe with Seizures / Preventing SUDEP
Epilepsy Action: Safety advice for people with epilepsy

title: Depression and SSRI counselling
summary: When starting an SSRI for depression, clear counselling improves adherence and safety. Key messages: the antidepressant effect is delayed (weeks); some side effects occur early and often settle; suicidal thoughts may increase early (especially in young people); and the drug must not be stopped abruptly.

sections.heading: Key counselling points
items: Delayed benefit: mood improvement usually takes a few weeks (often 2-4 weeks to start, with fuller benefit by ~6-8 weeks at therapeutic dose) - keep taking it even if you feel no better at first
Early side effects: nausea, GI upset, headache, restlessness/anxiety, and sleep changes are common early and often settle within ~1-2 weeks
Suicidality: there can be a small increase in suicidal thoughts early in treatment, particularly in those under 25 - arrange early review and clear safety-netting
Do NOT stop abruptly: stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms - any planned stop should be a gradual, supervised taper

steps.detail: Review within ~1-2 weeks of starting (and sooner / more closely in under-25s or those at higher risk); assess response, side effects and suicidality.
Tell the patient what to do if thoughts of self-harm worsen, continue treatment for an adequate period after recovery to reduce relapse, and taper rather than stop suddenly when discontinuing.

redFlags: New or worsening suicidal thoughts, agitation, or self-harm (especially early and in under-25s) - urgent review
Features of serotonin syndrome (agitation, tremor, sweating, fever, clonus) - especially with other serotonergic drugs - urgent assessment
Abrupt discontinuation causing discontinuation symptoms

references.label: NICE NG222: Depression in adults - treatment and management

title: Lifestyle and cardiovascular-risk counselling
summary: Lifestyle change is the foundation of cardiovascular disease prevention. Counselling targets the modifiable risk factors - smoking, diet, physical activity, weight, alcohol, blood pressure, lipids and glucose - alongside formal risk assessment to guide whether drug therapy (e.g. a statin) is also indicated.

sections.heading: Modifiable risk factors to address
items: Smoking: the single most important modifiable risk - offer cessation support (the strongest lifestyle intervention)
Diet: more fruit/vegetables, wholegrains, oily fish and unsaturated fats; reduce salt, saturated/trans fat and sugary foods
Physical activity: aim for the recommended level (e.g. ~150 minutes/week of moderate activity) plus reducing sedentary time
Weight: achieve/maintain a healthy weight and waist circumference
Alcohol: keep within recommended low-risk limits
Manage blood pressure, lipids and diabetes; assess CVD risk with a validated tool (e.g. QRISK) to guide statin/other therapy

steps.detail: Calculate cardiovascular risk and tailor advice to the individual's risk factors, readiness to change and circumstances; agree realistic goals.

steps.step: Support change and combine with treatment
steps.detail: Use behaviour-change support and follow-up; lifestyle advice complements (does not replace) indicated drug therapy such as statins or antihypertensives.

redFlags: Established CVD or very high estimated risk - ensure secondary prevention (e.g. statin, antiplatelet/BP control as indicated), not lifestyle advice alone
Chest pain on exertion, breathlessness, or other cardiac symptoms - assess/refer, do not treat as lifestyle counselling only
Severe hypertension or markedly abnormal lipids/glucose - act promptly

references.label: NICE CG181: Cardiovascular disease - risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification
WHO Cardiovascular diseases fact sheet (risk factors)

title: Alcohol brief intervention (FRAMES)
summary: A brief intervention is a short (typically 5-15 minute) structured conversation, usually after screening (e.g. AUDIT), to help someone with risky or harmful alcohol use cut down. The FRAMES model summarises its effective components; brief interventions reduce consumption in non-dependent drinkers.

sections.heading: FRAMES components
items: Feedback: give personalised feedback on the person's drinking and its risks/harms (e.g. from the screening result)
Responsibility: emphasise that change is the person's own choice and responsibility
Advice: give clear advice to cut down or stop
Menu of options: offer a range of practical strategies/options to change
Empathy: use a warm, reflective, non-judgemental style (not confrontation)
Self-efficacy: build the person's confidence and belief that they can change

steps.detail: Screen with a validated tool (e.g. AUDIT / AUDIT-C); deliver the brief intervention to those with risky/harmful (non-dependent) use.
Brief intervention is for non-dependent drinkers; refer those with possible dependence or complex needs for specialist assessment and treatment (and manage withdrawal safely).

redFlags: Signs of alcohol dependence (craving, tolerance, withdrawal, loss of control) - refer for specialist assessment; brief intervention alone is insufficient
Risk of severe withdrawal / delirium tremens or withdrawal seizures - do not advise abrupt cessation without medical support
Co-existing depression, suicidality, or safeguarding concerns

references.label: FRAMES - brief intervention for risky or harmful alcohol consumption (DACAS)
WHO/ASSIST brief intervention for substance use (PMC review)

title: CHC in adequately controlled hypertension
summary: Combined hormonal contraception is WHO MEC Category 3 in adequately controlled hypertension; choose a progestogen-only method or copper IUD instead.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 (initiation and continuation) for adequately controlled hypertension where blood pressure can be assessed and is in target range on treatment.
Risks usually outweigh advantages because oestrogen further raises blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: Why
items: Oestrogen in CHC increases hepatic angiotensinogen production and modestly raises blood pressure.
Even controlled hypertension carries baseline elevated cardiovascular and stroke risk that CHC compounds.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer progestogen-only pill, DMPA (if BP <160/100), implant, LNG-IUD or copper IUD - all Category 1 or 2 in controlled hypertension.
Reassess blood pressure at every visit if a Category 3 method is used because other options are unacceptable.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in hypertension with SBP 140-159 or DBP 90-99 mmHg
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3 in hypertension at SBP 140-159 or DBP 90-99 mmHg; use a progestogen-only method or copper IUD.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for systolic BP 140-159 mmHg or diastolic 90-99 mmHg.
Risks usually outweigh benefits - avoid initiation; consider switching if already on CHC.

sections.heading: Why
items: Oestrogen exacerbates hypertension and increases stroke and myocardial infarction risk in a dose-dependent fashion.
Absolute risk rises with baseline BP, age and smoking.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to POP, implant, LNG-IUD or copper IUD (all Category 1).
DMPA is Category 2 in this BP range and is acceptable if other options are unsuitable.
Treat hypertension to target before reconsidering hormonal methods.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in severe hypertension (SBP >=160 or DBP >=100 mmHg) or vascular disease
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in severe hypertension or known vascular disease - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 (unacceptable risk) for SBP >=160 mmHg, DBP >=100 mmHg, or hypertension with vascular disease.
Method must NOT be initiated or continued.

sections.heading: Why
items: Severe hypertension already confers high stroke and acute coronary syndrome risk; adding oestrogen substantially increases that risk.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1), LNG-IUD (Category 2) or progestogen-only pill/implant.
DMPA is Category 3 in severe hypertension - avoid unless no alternative is available.
Refer for blood pressure control before counselling on hormonal options.

redFlags: Initiating or continuing CHC at SBP >=160 or DBP >=100 mmHg - unacceptable cardiovascular risk.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in women aged >=35 smoking <15 cigarettes/day
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3 in women aged 35 or older who smoke fewer than 15 cigarettes per day - avoid.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for women aged >=35 smoking <15 cigarettes/day.
Risks usually outweigh advantages.

sections.heading: Why
items: Smoking and age >=35 each independently raise cardiovascular events; oestrogen multiplies the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUD or copper IUD (all Category 1).
Use the consultation to offer smoking-cessation support.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in women aged >=35 smoking >=15 cigarettes/day
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in women aged 35 or older who smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for women aged >=35 smoking >=15 cigarettes/day.

sections.heading: Why
items: Combined effect of age, heavy smoking and oestrogen produces unacceptable risk of arterial thrombosis, MI and stroke.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods (POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUD or copper IUD - all Category 1).
Offer evidence-based smoking-cessation support; reassess CHC eligibility only after cessation.

redFlags: Continuing CHC in heavy smokers >=35 - stop and switch.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in current/acute venous thromboembolism (on anticoagulation)
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in current VTE even while on anticoagulation - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for acute DVT/PE and for established VTE on anticoagulant therapy.

sections.heading: Why
items: Oestrogen increases coagulation factor synthesis (II, VII, X, fibrinogen) and decreases protein S; risk of recurrent thrombosis is unacceptable even with therapeutic anticoagulation.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1) or progestogen-only methods - POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUD all Category 2 in VTE on anticoagulation.
Avoid DMPA at the time of initiating anticoagulation if there is concern about intramuscular haematoma; subcutaneous DMPA is an alternative.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in personal history of VTE (not on current anticoagulation)
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in personal history of VTE - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for past DVT/PE regardless of ongoing risk factors.

sections.heading: Why
items: Recurrent VTE risk is substantially elevated in those with prior events; oestrogen further raises that risk to unacceptable levels.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer POP, implant, LNG-IUD (all Category 2) or copper IUD (Category 1).
DMPA is Category 2 in past VTE and is acceptable.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in known thrombogenic mutation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency)
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in known thrombogenic mutations - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein S, protein C and antithrombin deficiencies.

sections.heading: Why
items: Inherited thrombophilias already confer 5-50x baseline VTE risk; oestrogen multiplies this further.
Routine screening for thrombophilia before CHC is NOT recommended (low prevalence, poor cost-effectiveness) but a known diagnosis is a clear contraindication.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUD all Category 2) or copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in migraine with aura at any age
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in migraine with aura at any age - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for migraine with aura at any age, including for continuation.
Stop CHC immediately if new aura develops.

sections.heading: Why
items: Migraine with aura is an independent risk factor for ischaemic stroke; oestrogen approximately doubles that risk.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP (Category 2 initiation, 3 continuation), implant or LNG-IUD (Category 2), DMPA (Category 2) or copper IUD (Category 1).
Document the aura history clearly so future clinicians do not restart CHC.

redFlags: New focal neurology, visual aura or sensory aura while on CHC - stop CHC and assess for stroke.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in migraine without aura, age <35
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 2 for initiation and Category 3 for continuation in migraine without aura under 35.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for initiation, Category 3 for continuation in migraine without aura age <35.

sections.heading: Why
items: Background stroke risk in migraine without aura is lower, but CHC modestly increases it; re-evaluation is needed if migraines change.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Counsel to report any new aura, focal symptoms, or worsening headache - if these occur, stop CHC.
Consider switching to POP, implant or LNG-IUD if headaches worsen on CHC.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in migraine without aura, age >=35
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3 in migraine without aura at age 35 or older - avoid; switch method.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for initiation and continuation in migraine without aura age >=35.

sections.heading: Why
items: Age, migraine and oestrogen combine to raise stroke risk above an acceptable threshold.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer POP, implant, LNG-IUD, DMPA (all Category 1-2) or copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC and breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in breastfeeding women less than 6 weeks postpartum - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for breastfeeding women <6 weeks postpartum.
Category 3 from 6 weeks to <6 months postpartum if breastfeeding.

sections.heading: Why
items: Postpartum period is a hypercoagulable state; oestrogen further elevates VTE risk.
Oestrogen also reduces breast milk volume and may shorten breastfeeding duration.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP, implant or LNG-IUD (Category 2 at <6 weeks, Category 1 after) - all compatible with breastfeeding.
Copper IUD can be inserted at delivery or after 4 weeks postpartum.
DMPA is Category 3 at <6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC postpartum, not breastfeeding
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 at <21 days, Category 3 at 21-42 days (with other VTE risk factors), and Category 2 from 42 days postpartum in non-breastfeeding women.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: <21 days postpartum: Category 4 (do not use).

21-42 days postpartum without VTE risk factors: Category 2; with VTE risk factors (age >=35, prior VTE, thrombophilia, smoking, BMI >=30, peripartum cardiomyopathy, postpartum haemorrhage, transfusion, caesarean): Category 3.
>=42 days postpartum: Category 2.

sections.heading: Why
items: VTE risk is markedly elevated for the first 6 weeks postpartum and oestrogen amplifies it.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP or implant from birth (Category 1).
Copper IUD or LNG-IUD can be inserted within 48 hours postpartum or after 4 weeks.
Counsel that fertility may return as early as 21 days postpartum.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in diabetes with vascular complications or duration >20 years
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3 or 4 in diabetes with vascular disease - avoid.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3/4 for diabetes with nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy or other vascular disease, or duration >20 years (severity determines 3 vs 4).
Category 2 for uncomplicated diabetes.

sections.heading: Why
items: Oestrogen worsens arterial thrombotic risk in diabetes-related vasculopathy.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP, implant, LNG-IUD (Category 2) or copper IUD (Category 1).
DMPA is Category 3 in vascular diabetes.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC with multiple cardiovascular risk factors
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3/4 when multiple cardiovascular risk factors (age, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity) coexist.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 or 4 (severity-dependent) when several CV risk factors are present simultaneously.

sections.heading: Why
items: Risk factors act multiplicatively; oestrogen adds further arterial event risk.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP, implant, LNG-IUD or copper IUD - all Category 2 or below.
Address modifiable risk factors (BP, lipids, weight, smoking).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in current/history of stroke or ischaemic heart disease
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in current or past stroke or ischaemic heart disease - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for current and past ischaemic stroke or IHD.

sections.heading: Why
items: Oestrogen increases recurrent arterial thrombotic events.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP (Category 2/3), implant (Category 2/3), LNG-IUD (Category 2) or copper IUD (Category 1).
DMPA is Category 3 in past stroke or IHD.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in current breast cancer
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 4 in current breast cancer - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for current breast cancer.
Category 3 for past breast cancer with no recurrence for 5+ years.

sections.heading: Why
items: Breast cancer is hormone-sensitive; hormonal contraception may worsen prognosis.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1).
All hormonal methods including POP, implant, DMPA and LNG-IUD are Category 4 in current breast cancer.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC in acute viral hepatitis, severe cirrhosis or hepatocellular adenoma/carcinoma
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3-4 in significant liver disease - avoid.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for initiation in acute viral hepatitis (Category 2 for continuation).
Category 4 in severe (decompensated) cirrhosis, hepatocellular adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Category 1 in mild (compensated) cirrhosis.

sections.heading: Why
items: CHC is hepatically metabolised; oestrogen can worsen cholestasis and promote growth of vascular hepatic tumours.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1) or progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUD - all Category 3 in severe cirrhosis and adenoma).
Reassess if hepatitis resolves or liver function improves.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Progestogen-only pill in breastfeeding women
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 1 from 6 weeks postpartum and Category 2 before 6 weeks - safe for breastfeeding.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum.
Category 1 from 6 weeks postpartum onwards.

sections.heading: Why
items: Progestogens do not reduce milk supply and minimal amounts are transferred to the infant; long-term infant outcomes are reassuring.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: POP can usually be started from birth in resource-limited settings to maximise contraceptive coverage.
Counsel on strict daily timing (same time each day for traditional POP; 12-hour window for desogestrel).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in current VTE on anticoagulation
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 2 in current or past VTE - acceptable with monitoring.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for acute DVT/PE on anticoagulation and for history of VTE.

sections.heading: Why
items: POP has minimal effect on clotting factors and does not raise VTE risk meaningfully.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: POP is a reasonable option for women needing contraception while on long-term anticoagulation.
Copper IUD remains Category 1 if non-hormonal is preferred.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in migraine with aura
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 2 for initiation and Category 3 for continuation in migraine with aura.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Initiation Category 2, continuation Category 3 if aura develops or persists.

sections.heading: Why
items: Progestogens carry a small but uncertain stroke signal relative to non-hormonal methods in migraine with aura.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Copper IUD (Category 1) is preferred when contraception is non-urgent.
Reassess if aura frequency or severity changes.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in current breast cancer
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 4 in current breast cancer - do not use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for current breast cancer.
Category 3 for past breast cancer disease-free for 5 years.

sections.heading: Why
items: Breast cancer can be hormone-sensitive; even progestogen alone is considered to confer unacceptable risk in active disease.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in severe cirrhosis or hepatocellular tumour
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 3 in severe (decompensated) cirrhosis, hepatocellular adenoma and HCC.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 in severe decompensated cirrhosis, hepatocellular adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Category 1 in mild cirrhosis.

sections.heading: Why
items: Progestogens are hepatically metabolised and may aggravate cholestasis or vascular hepatic tumour growth.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1) where possible.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP with rifampicin or rifabutin
summary: POP efficacy is reduced by rifampicin/rifabutin (CYP3A4 induction) - WHO MEC Category 3; choose a non-affected method.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 with rifampicin or rifabutin therapy (e.g. TB treatment).

sections.heading: Why
items: Rifamycins are potent CYP3A4 inducers and accelerate progestogen metabolism, reducing contraceptive levels.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to DMPA, copper IUD or LNG-IUD (all unaffected, Category 1-2) for the duration of rifamycin therapy and for 28 days after stopping.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP with enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, topiramate, oxcarbazepine, primidone)
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 3 with enzyme-inducing antiepileptics; choose DMPA or an IUD.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 with phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, topiramate (>=200 mg/day), oxcarbazepine.

sections.heading: Why
items: CYP3A4 induction reduces serum progestogen and contraceptive efficacy.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use DMPA (Category 1), copper IUD (Category 1) or LNG-IUD (Category 1).
Lamotrigine alone does not induce contraceptive metabolism (POP Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in current ischaemic heart disease or stroke
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 2 for initiation and Category 3 for continuation in current IHD or stroke.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Initiation Category 2; continuation Category 3 if IHD or stroke develops while on POP.

sections.heading: Why
items: Small theoretical effect on lipid profile and arterial events; uncertainty drives a more cautious continuation rating.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to copper IUD (Category 1) or LNG-IUD (Category 2).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in unexplained vaginal bleeding (suspicious for serious condition)
summary: POP is WHO MEC Category 2 in unexplained vaginal bleeding - acceptable while investigating.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for unexplained vaginal bleeding pending evaluation.

sections.heading: Why
items: POP does not mask or worsen the underlying pathology but irregular bleeding on POP may complicate assessment.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Evaluate the cause before relying on POP long-term; consider transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling per local guidelines.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: POP in HIV on antiretroviral therapy
summary: POP is generally WHO MEC Category 1-2 with most ART regimens; efavirenz reduces progestogen levels - Category 2.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 1-2 with most ART.
Category 2 with efavirenz, nevirapine, ritonavir-boosted PIs (modestly reduced progestogen exposure).

sections.heading: Why
items: Some NNRTIs and PIs induce hepatic metabolism of progestogens, lowering serum levels.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Counsel on consistent daily use; consider DMPA, LNG-IUD or copper IUD (Category 1) if adherence is a concern.
Always promote condom use for HIV/STI prevention.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 2 in breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum per the 6th edition (revised from Category 3 in the 5th edition).

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum (WHO MEC 6th ed, 2024).
Category 1 from 6 weeks postpartum onwards.

sections.heading: Why
items: Evidence shows no clinically meaningful impact of DMPA on breastfeeding outcomes when started in the early postpartum period.
WHO MEC 6th ed liberalised this category from prior editions.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: DMPA can be started immediately postpartum in breastfeeding women where benefit outweighs theoretical concerns.
Counsel on injection schedule and warn of irregular bleeding in early months.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in severe hypertension (SBP >=160 or DBP >=100 mmHg)
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 3 in severe hypertension (SBP >=160 or DBP >=100) - avoid; use a non-hormonal or non-injectable method.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for SBP >=160 or DBP >=100 mmHg.
Category 2 in adequately controlled hypertension or BP 140-159/90-99.

sections.heading: Why
items: DMPA may have modest adverse vascular effects via lipid changes and the inability to discontinue quickly if BP rises.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1), LNG-IUD (Category 2), POP or implant (Category 2).
Treat hypertension to target before re-considering DMPA.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in personal history of VTE
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 2 in past or current VTE - acceptable.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for past DVT/PE and for current DVT/PE on anticoagulation.

sections.heading: Why
items: DMPA has minimal pro-thrombotic effect compared with oestrogen-containing methods.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: DMPA is a reasonable choice for women who cannot use CHC because of VTE.
Consider subcutaneous DMPA if there is concern about intramuscular haematoma in those on anticoagulation.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA with multiple cardiovascular risk factors
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 3 when multiple cardiovascular risk factors coexist.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 when multiple risk factors (older age, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia) are simultaneously present.

sections.heading: Why
items: Adverse effects on HDL-C and inability to discontinue quickly underlie the cautious rating.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1), LNG-IUD or implant (Category 2).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in diabetes with vascular complications or duration >20 years
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 3 in diabetes with vascular complications or long duration.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 in diabetes with nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy or duration >20 years.
Category 2 in uncomplicated diabetes.

sections.heading: Why
items: Concerns relate to lipid effects and slow reversibility.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1), LNG-IUD (Category 2) or implant (Category 2).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in current or past stroke or ischaemic heart disease
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 3 in current or past stroke or IHD.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for current and past ischaemic stroke and IHD (initiation and continuation).

sections.heading: Why
items: Possible adverse effect on HDL-C and prolonged duration of action support avoiding DMPA.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1), LNG-IUD (Category 2) or POP/implant (Category 2-3).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in current breast cancer
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 4 in current breast cancer.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 in current breast cancer.
Category 3 in past breast cancer disease-free for 5 years.

sections.heading: Why
items: Breast cancer may be hormone-sensitive; long-acting injectable progestogen poses unacceptable risk.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in severe cirrhosis or hepatic tumour
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 3 in severe cirrhosis, hepatocellular adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 in decompensated cirrhosis, hepatic adenoma and HCC.
Category 1 in mild cirrhosis.

sections.heading: Why
items: Hepatic metabolism and theoretical tumour growth concerns.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in unexplained vaginal bleeding (before evaluation)
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 3 for initiation in unexplained vaginal bleeding suspicious for serious condition - evaluate first.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for initiation in unexplained vaginal bleeding pending evaluation.
Category 2 for continuation if bleeding develops on DMPA.

sections.heading: Why
items: DMPA itself causes irregular bleeding and may delay diagnosis of underlying pathology (endometrial cancer, GTD, cervical disease).

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Investigate the cause (history, examination, imaging, endometrial sampling) before starting DMPA.
Copper IUD is also Category 4 in unexplained bleeding - establish a diagnosis first.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA and bone mineral density (adolescents and women >45)
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 2 in adolescents (<18) and in women >45 because of reversible bone density loss.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 in adolescents <18 years and women >45 years.
Category 1 in 18-45 year olds without bone disease.

sections.heading: Why
items: DMPA suppresses oestrogen and causes a reversible reduction in bone mineral density; the FDA-style black box warning is reflected in the cautious rating at age extremes.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Counsel on adequate calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise.
Do not restrict duration of DMPA solely on bone concerns - benefits typically outweigh risks - but review choice periodically.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA with rifampicin or enzyme-inducing antiepileptics
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 1 with rifampicin and enzyme-inducing antiepileptics - efficacy preserved.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 1 with rifampicin, rifabutin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, topiramate, oxcarbazepine.

sections.heading: Why
items: DMPA serum levels far exceed contraceptive thresholds, so CYP3A4 induction does not meaningfully reduce efficacy.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: DMPA is a preferred hormonal option for women on rifamycins or enzyme-inducing AEDs.
Standard 12- to 13-weekly injection schedule applies.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: DMPA in HIV on antiretroviral therapy
summary: DMPA is WHO MEC Category 1 with all ART regimens.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 1 with all ART including efavirenz-based regimens.

sections.heading: Why
items: Drug interaction studies show DMPA efficacy is not reduced by NNRTIs or PIs.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: DMPA is a preferred hormonal option in women on efavirenz where implant efficacy concerns exist.
Continue condom use for HIV/STI prevention.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Etonogestrel/levonorgestrel implant in breastfeeding women
summary: The contraceptive implant is WHO MEC Category 2 in breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum and Category 1 from 6 weeks.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 in breastfeeding women <6 weeks postpartum.
Category 1 from 6 weeks postpartum.

sections.heading: Why
items: Progestogen-only implants do not impair milk volume or quality.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Implants can be inserted immediately postpartum in many settings to maximise contraceptive uptake.
Counsel on irregular bleeding, especially in the first 3-6 months.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant in current or past VTE
summary: Implant is WHO MEC Category 2 in current and past VTE - acceptable.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 for current VTE on anticoagulation and past VTE.

sections.heading: Why
items: Implant has no clinically significant effect on coagulation factors.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Implant is a good option for women who cannot use CHC because of VTE.
Insertion site bruising/haematoma is the main practical concern with concurrent anticoagulation - apply firm pressure.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant in current breast cancer
summary: Implant is WHO MEC Category 4 in current breast cancer.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 for current breast cancer.
Category 3 for past breast cancer disease-free for 5 years.

sections.heading: Why
items: Hormone-sensitive disease.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant in severe cirrhosis or hepatic tumour
summary: Implant is WHO MEC Category 3 in severe (decompensated) cirrhosis, hepatocellular adenoma and HCC.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 in decompensated cirrhosis, hepatic adenoma and HCC.
Category 1 in mild cirrhosis.

sections.heading: Why
items: Hepatic metabolism of etonogestrel/levonorgestrel and concern for tumour growth.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use copper IUD (Category 1).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant with rifampicin/rifabutin
summary: Implant efficacy is reduced by rifampicin - WHO MEC Category 2 but consider alternative method.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 with rifampicin or rifabutin.

sections.heading: Why
items: Rifamycins induce CYP3A4 and lower etonogestrel levels; contraceptive failures have been reported.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to DMPA, copper IUD or LNG-IUD (all Category 1) for the duration of rifamycin therapy and 28 days after.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant with enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs
summary: Implant is WHO MEC Category 2 with enzyme-inducing AEDs but efficacy may be reduced; prefer DMPA or IUD.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 with phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, topiramate, oxcarbazepine.

sections.heading: Why
items: CYP3A4 induction reduces etonogestrel levels; pregnancies have been reported.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use DMPA, copper IUD or LNG-IUD (all Category 1).
Lamotrigine alone does not require switching - implant is Category 1 with lamotrigine.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant with lamotrigine monotherapy
summary: Implant is WHO MEC Category 1 with lamotrigine monotherapy - no interaction.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 1 with lamotrigine monotherapy.

sections.heading: Why
items: Lamotrigine is not a CYP3A4 inducer and does not affect etonogestrel levels.
Unlike CHC, the implant does not lower lamotrigine serum levels, so seizure control is preserved.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Implant is a preferred hormonal option in women with epilepsy on lamotrigine.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Implant in HIV on efavirenz-based ART
summary: Implant efficacy may be reduced by efavirenz - WHO MEC Category 2; counsel and consider alternative.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 with efavirenz-based ART.

sections.heading: Why
items: Efavirenz induces CYP3A4 and lowers etonogestrel and levonorgestrel implant levels; contraceptive failures are documented.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to DMPA, copper IUD or LNG-IUD (all Category 1) in women on efavirenz where pregnancy avoidance is critical.
Dolutegravir does not induce these enzymes - implant Category 1 with dolutegravir-based ART.
Continue condoms for HIV transmission prevention.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: LNG-IUD postpartum insertion timing
summary: LNG-IUD is WHO MEC Category 1 if inserted <48 hours postpartum, Category 3 between 48 hours and 4 weeks, and Category 1 from 4 weeks.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: <48 hours postpartum (including post-placental and at caesarean): Category 1-2.
48 hours to <4 weeks postpartum: Category 3.
>=4 weeks postpartum: Category 1.

sections.heading: Why
items: Risk of expulsion is highest at 48 hours to 4 weeks postpartum; immediate or delayed insertion is safer.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Insert at delivery or after 4 weeks postpartum to minimise expulsion.
Counsel postpartum women on this window.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: LNG-IUD in puerperal sepsis
summary: LNG-IUD is WHO MEC Category 4 in puerperal sepsis - do not insert.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 (initiation) in puerperal sepsis.

sections.heading: Why
items: Insertion would aggravate established uterine infection.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Treat infection fully; consider IUD only after complete resolution.
Counsel on alternative methods (POP, implant, DMPA, condoms) in the meantime.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: LNG-IUD immediately after septic abortion
summary: LNG-IUD is WHO MEC Category 4 immediately after septic abortion - do not insert.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 4 immediately post-septic abortion.
Category 1 after uncomplicated first or second trimester abortion.

sections.heading: Why
items: Insertion into an infected uterus risks ascending infection and uterine perforation.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Treat infection; reassess after complete clinical recovery.
Use interim contraception (POP, condoms, implant).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

summary: LNG-IUD is WHO MEC Category 4 for initiation in unexplained vaginal bleeding suspicious for serious condition (Category 2 for continuation).

items: Category 4 for initiation in unexplained vaginal bleeding pending evaluation.

items: Insertion would interfere with diagnosis of malignancy or other serious pathology.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Investigate before insertion (history, examination, pelvic ultrasound, endometrial sampling per local protocol).
Once benign cause is established (or treated), proceed.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: LNG-IUD in current pelvic inflammatory disease
summary: LNG-IUD is WHO MEC Category 4 for initiation and Category 2 for continuation in current PID.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Initiation Category 4 in current PID.

sections.heading: Why
items: Inserting into an infected upper genital tract worsens infection; an established IUD does not need removal if PID is treated.

items: Treat PID first; defer insertion until full clinical recovery (typically 3 months).

title: LNG-IUD with past PID (without subsequent pregnancy)

items: Test for gonorrhoea/chlamydia before or at insertion in high-prevalence settings.

title: LNG-IUD with cervical cancer awaiting treatment

Coordinate with the oncology team.
