sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: No medical condition for which risks outweigh benefits of a single dose of LNG-EC or UPA-EC.
Category 1 for repeated use as well, but routine contraception is preferred.

sections.heading: Why
items: Single short hormone exposure; serious adverse effects are not documented.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer LNG 1.5 mg up to 72 hours (some efficacy to 120 hours) after unprotected sex.
Offer UPA 30 mg up to 120 hours after unprotected sex.
Counsel on starting ongoing contraception and on copper IUD as the most effective EC option.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Emergency contraceptive pills in higher body weight/BMI
summary: ECP efficacy may be reduced at higher body weight; copper IUD is the most reliable EC method.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: LNG-EC and UPA-EC remain Category 1 at all weights but efficacy data suggest reduced effectiveness at higher BMI (>26 kg/m2 for LNG; >35 kg/m2 for UPA).

sections.heading: Why
items: Pharmacokinetic dilution and possible reduced ovulation suppression at higher body weight.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer copper IUD within 5 days (most effective EC, unaffected by weight).
If pill EC is chosen, UPA outperforms LNG at higher BMI; consider double-dose LNG if UPA unavailable.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Repeat use of emergency contraceptive pills in the same cycle
summary: Repeat ECP use is WHO MEC Category 1 - safe; do not deny EC because of recent prior use.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 1 for repeat use of LNG-EC or UPA-EC.

sections.heading: Why
items: There is no safety reason to withhold EC; the priority is preventing unintended pregnancy.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Counsel on ongoing reliable contraception.
Do not mix LNG-EC and UPA-EC within the same cycle - antagonism reduces efficacy.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Emergency contraceptive pills while breastfeeding
summary: LNG-EC is WHO MEC Category 1 in breastfeeding; UPA-EC requires temporary interruption of breastfeeding for 1 week.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: LNG-EC Category 1 in breastfeeding.
UPA-EC: limited data; advise discarding breast milk for 24 hours (per some labels, up to 1 week).

sections.heading: Why
items: LNG transfers in negligible amounts; UPA transfer is uncertain.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Prefer LNG-EC or copper IUD in breastfeeding women.
If UPA is used, express and discard milk per local guidance (commonly 24 hours).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: UPA-EC in severe asthma on oral glucocorticoids
summary: UPA may be less suitable in severe asthma on oral glucocorticoids - prefer LNG-EC or copper IUD.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: UPA-EC: caution in severe asthma uncontrolled by oral glucocorticoids (manufacturer advice).
LNG-EC Category 1.

sections.heading: Why
items: UPA is a selective progesterone receptor modulator with theoretical antagonism of glucocorticoid effects.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use LNG-EC or insert copper IUD within 5 days.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Emergency contraceptive pills with enzyme inducers (rifampicin, AEDs, St John's Wort)
summary: Efficacy of LNG-EC and UPA-EC is reduced by enzyme-inducing drugs; double the LNG dose or use copper IUD.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: No formal MEC category but pharmacokinetic data show reduced ECP exposure with CYP3A4 inducers.

sections.heading: Why
items: Rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, St John's Wort and efavirenz induce CYP3A4 and lower LNG/UPA concentrations.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Copper IUD is the preferred EC method.
If pill EC is used, double the LNG dose to 3 mg.
UPA effectiveness in this setting is unknown - avoid if possible.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Copper IUD as emergency contraception
summary: Copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception (>99% effective) and can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected sex or 5 days after estimated ovulation.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: WHO MEC Category 1 in most women; usual MEC conditions for Cu-IUD apply (e.g. Category 4 in current PID or unexplained vaginal bleeding).

sections.heading: Why
items: Copper is spermicidal and prevents fertilisation and implantation.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Offer Cu-IUD to all eligible women seeking EC, especially those with higher BMI, those on enzyme inducers, and those wanting ongoing contraception.
Screen and treat for STIs at insertion if individual risk is high.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Post-EC counselling and ongoing contraception (quick start)
summary: Quick-starting ongoing contraception immediately after ECP is safe and effective; timing differs for UPA vs LNG.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Hormonal contraception (CHC, POP, implant, DMPA) can be started immediately after LNG-EC (no waiting).
After UPA-EC, wait 5 days before starting hormonal methods (UPA and progestogens compete at the progesterone receptor).

sections.heading: Why
items: UPA's antagonist activity is blocked by simultaneous progestogen exposure, reducing UPA's efficacy.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use condoms or abstinence for 7 days (5 days wait + 2 days backup) after UPA before relying on a new hormonal method.
Perform a pregnancy test 3 weeks after EC if no menses.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC with lamotrigine monotherapy
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3 with lamotrigine monotherapy due to bidirectional interaction - prefer progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 for CHC with lamotrigine monotherapy.

sections.heading: Why
items: Oestrogen induces UGT glucuronidation of lamotrigine, lowering its serum level by up to 50% - increasing seizure risk on active CHC weeks and risk of toxicity on pill-free week.
Lamotrigine does not meaningfully reduce CHC contraceptive efficacy.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Use POP, implant, LNG-IUD, DMPA or copper IUD (all Category 1 with lamotrigine).
If CHC must be used, the seizure team should monitor lamotrigine levels and consider continuous (no pill-free interval) dosing.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC with rifampicin or rifabutin
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 3 with rifampicin/rifabutin - efficacy reduced; switch method.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 3 with rifampicin and rifabutin (initiation and continuation).

sections.heading: Why
items: Rifamycins are potent CYP3A4 inducers that markedly reduce ethinyl oestradiol and progestogen levels.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to DMPA, copper IUD or LNG-IUD (all Category 1) for the duration of rifamycin therapy and 28 days after.
Common scenario in TB programmes - integrate contraception counselling at TB initiation.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: CHC with efavirenz-based ART
summary: CHC is WHO MEC Category 2 with efavirenz but contraceptive efficacy is reduced; consider alternative.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Category 2 with efavirenz-based ART.

sections.heading: Why
items: Efavirenz induces CYP3A4 and lowers ethinyl oestradiol and progestogen levels; contraceptive failures documented.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to DMPA, copper IUD or LNG-IUD (all Category 1) in women requiring highly reliable contraception.
Dolutegravir-based regimens do not require switching - CHC Category 1.
Continue condoms for HIV transmission prevention.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Contraceptive choice in the postpartum period - quick reference
summary: Method choice postpartum depends on breastfeeding status, time since delivery and VTE risk; POP, implant and LNG-IUD (after 4 weeks) suit most women.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Birth to 21 days: avoid CHC (Category 4 in all due to VTE); POP/implant Category 1-2; LNG/Cu IUD Category 1-2 if <48 h or Category 3 if 48 h-4 weeks.
21-42 days non-breastfeeding without VTE risk factors: CHC Category 2; with risk factors Category 3.
>=42 days non-breastfeeding: CHC Category 2.
Breastfeeding <6 weeks: CHC Category 4, POP/implant Category 2, DMPA Category 2 (WHO MEC 6th ed).

sections.heading: Why
items: VTE risk peaks in the first 6 weeks postpartum; expulsion risk for IUDs is highest from 48 h to 4 weeks.
Breastfeeding interaction with oestrogen historically restricted CHC use.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Recommend POP, implant or LNG/Cu IUD (at delivery or after 4 weeks) for breastfeeding mothers.
Discuss return-to-fertility (as early as day 21 non-breastfeeding).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Contraceptive choice in women on antiretroviral therapy - quick reference
summary: Most contraceptives are MEC Category 1-2 with ART; the main interaction concerns are efavirenz lowering implant/CHC efficacy.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: DMPA, Cu-IUD, LNG-IUD: Category 1 with all ART.
Implant with efavirenz: Category 2 (reduced efficacy).
CHC with efavirenz: Category 2 (reduced efficacy).
POP with efavirenz: Category 2.

sections.heading: Why
items: Efavirenz and some PIs induce CYP3A4, reducing hormonal contraceptive levels.
Dolutegravir, raltegravir, tenofovir and lamivudine do not induce CYP3A4.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Prefer DMPA, Cu-IUD or LNG-IUD in women on efavirenz-based regimens.
Always promote condoms for HIV/STI prevention regardless of method.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Contraceptive choice during TB treatment with rifampicin - quick reference
summary: Rifampicin substantially reduces CHC, POP, implant and ECP efficacy; DMPA, Cu-IUD and LNG-IUD are reliable alternatives.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: CHC, POP: Category 3 with rifampicin/rifabutin.
Implant: Category 2 (efficacy reduced).
DMPA, Cu-IUD, LNG-IUD: Category 1.

sections.heading: Why
items: Rifamycins are potent CYP3A4 inducers.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Switch to DMPA, Cu-IUD or LNG-IUD for the duration of TB therapy plus 28 days after stopping rifampicin.
For EC, prefer Cu-IUD or double LNG-EC dose (3 mg).
Integrate family planning counselling into TB services.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: Contraceptive choice with enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs - quick reference
summary: Enzyme-inducing AEDs reduce CHC, POP and implant efficacy; lamotrigine has a unique CHC interaction; DMPA and IUDs are safe.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, topiramate, oxcarbazepine: CHC Category 3, POP Category 3, implant Category 2, DMPA Category 1, Cu-IUD and LNG-IUD Category 1.
Lamotrigine monotherapy: CHC Category 3 (lamotrigine levels fall on CHC); all other methods Category 1.

sections.heading: Why
items: Most AEDs induce CYP3A4 reducing hormonal contraceptive levels; lamotrigine itself is induced by oestrogen.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Prefer DMPA, Cu-IUD or LNG-IUD in women on enzyme-inducing AEDs.
In lamotrigine monotherapy, implant or IUD are preferred over CHC to keep lamotrigine levels stable.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)

title: MCH family planning quick reference - method by clinical situation
summary: Quick reference matrix of preferred methods for common clinical situations encountered in Kenyan MCH clinics.

sections.heading: WHO MEC category
items: Hypertension (any severity): copper IUD, LNG-IUD or POP/implant; avoid CHC and use DMPA only if mild and BP <160/100.
Migraine with aura: avoid all CHC (Category 4); use POP/implant/LNG-IUD or Cu-IUD.
Past or current VTE: avoid CHC; use Cu-IUD (Category 1), POP/implant/DMPA/LNG-IUD (Category 2).
Breastfeeding from birth: POP, implant or IUD; defer CHC at least until 6 weeks (and prefer permanent avoidance while exclusively breastfeeding).
On efavirenz or rifampicin: DMPA, Cu-IUD or LNG-IUD.

sections.heading: Why
items: Derived from WHO MEC 6th ed (2024) categories where the rating differs between methods - choose the method with the highest acceptable category.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
items: Document the contraindicating condition prominently in the chart to prevent inadvertent re-initiation of a Category 3-4 method.
Always combine method choice with STI counselling and condom promotion.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed (2024)
